Direct radio outreach vs radio plugging

By the RadioReach editorial team Published August 19, 2026 Reviewed August 19, 2026

Direct outreach costs you time and buys you control; a radio plugger costs money and buys you relationships and hours back. Pluggers have standing contacts at stations and know each programmer's tastes and schedule, which genuinely matters at commercial and national level. For college and community radio — the tier most open to independent artists — a well-written direct pitch from the artist competes perfectly well.

What a plugger actually does

A radio plugger — promoter, in American usage — pitches your record to stations on your behalf. The real product is their existing relationships: a programmer who already takes their calls, plus the judgement to know which stations will plausibly play your record and when to approach them in a release cycle. Good pluggers also absorb the follow-up, which is the part most artists abandon.

What a plugger cannot do is guarantee airplay. Buying a contact list does not guarantee airplay. Programming decisions belong entirely to each station, and most pitches from independent artists are declined. Stations decide programming, and a plugger who promises otherwise is describing something they do not control.

When hiring is the right call

Hire a promoter when you have a genuine commercial radio target, when a release has budget behind it and a fixed window, or when you simply will not do the follow-up yourself. That last one is not a character flaw — a campaign half-run is worse than one properly delegated, and the honest question is not whether you could do it but whether you will.

Run it yourself when your target is college, community and specialty radio, when your budget is small, or when you want relationships that survive past this release. Our free guide to getting on the radio and pitch templates cover the method; the longer DIY-versus-promoter guide goes deeper on the decision.

How to evaluate a plugger

Ask for recent, checkable station adds — not a list of logos. Ask which specific stations they intend to approach for your record and why. Ask what reporting you get. Be wary of guaranteed airplay, of "we know everyone" without names, of packages priced identically regardless of genre, and of anyone who cannot describe a campaign that failed. A credible promoter will tell you if your record is not ready or not a fit, and will decline the work.

We are not neutral here — we sell the self-directed alternative. But a good promoter is worth their fee for the right record, and buying a contact file because it is cheaper, when what you needed was a campaign run for you, is a false economy.

Limitations of this page

Promoter fees vary widely by market, genre and campaign scope; the "four figures" characterisation is a general industry range rather than a surveyed figure, and we have not audited promoter pricing. We sell a product used for direct outreach, which is a conflict of interest you should factor in.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get radio airplay without a plugger?

Yes, particularly at college, community and specialty stations, which routinely program unsigned artists and read direct pitches. Commercial rotation is much harder without industry relationships. The realistic path is to build a track record at the accessible tier first — our college radio guide covers how.

How much does a radio plugger cost?

Campaign fees are commonly in the four figures and vary by market, genre and scope, so treat any single number with suspicion and get written quotes. What you are buying is relationships and follow-up time, not a promise of airplay — no promoter controls programming decisions.
